ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Adversary-in-the-Middle

Adversaries may try to insert themselves between two or more interconnected devices by utilizing an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) technique, which facilitates subsequent actions like [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040), [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002), or replay attacks ([Exploitation for Credential Access](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1212)). By exploiting functionalities of common networking protocols, which dictate the flow of network traffic (e.g., ARP, DNS, LLMNR, etc.), adversaries can compel a device to send data through a system they control, enabling them to gather information or carry out further operations. (Citation: Rapid7 MiTM Basics)

For instance, adversaries might adjust victim DNS settings to facilitate other malicious activities, such as hindering or redirecting users from genuine websites and/or inserting additional malware. (Citation: ttint_rat)(Citation: dns_changer_trojans)(Citation: ad_blocker_with_miner) Additionally, adversaries can manipulate DNS and exploit their position to capture user credentials, including access tokens ([Steal Application Access Token](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528)) and session cookies ([Steal Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539)). (Citation: volexity_0day_sophos_FW)(Citation: Token tactics) [Downgrade Attack](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1689) techniques may also be employed to achieve an AiTM position by negotiating a less secure, outdated, or weaker version of a communication protocol (SSL/TLS) or encryption algorithm. (Citation: mitm_tls_downgrade_att)(Citation: taxonomy_downgrade_att_tls)(Citation: tlseminar_downgrade_att)

Moreover, adversaries can make use of the AiTM position to attempt to observe and/or alter traffic, as seen in [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002). They can establish a position akin to AiTM to block traffic from reaching its intended destination, potentially to weaken defenses and/or assist in a [Network Denial of Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498).

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Direct Network Flood

Adversaries may seek to induce a denial of service (DoS) by inundating a target with a substantial volume of network traffic. This DoS attack can impair the availability and functionality of the affected system(s) and network. [Direct Network Flood](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498/001) occurs when one or multiple systems direct a high volume of network packets toward the network of the targeted service. Any network protocol may potentially be exploited for flooding purposes. While stateless protocols like UDP or ICMP are frequently employed, stateful protocols such as TCP can also be utilized.

Network flooding attacks against services and networks are often carried out using botnets. Extensive botnets can produce a considerable amount of traffic from systems distributed across the global Internet. Adversaries might possess the means to develop and manage their own botnet infrastructure, or they might opt to lease time on an established botnet to execute an attack. In severe instances of distributed DoS (DDoS), numerous systems may be engaged to create the flood, requiring only minimal traffic from each to generate sufficient volume to overwhelm the target network. In such scenarios, differentiating DDoS traffic from valid clients becomes exceedingly challenging. Some of the most notorious DDoS flooding attacks, including the 2012 incidents that targeted major US banks, have employed botnets. (Citation: USNYAG IranianBotnet March 2016)

ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Network Service Discovery Adversaries may seek to obtain a list of services operating on remote hosts and local network infrastructure devices, including those potentially susceptible to remote software exploitation. Common techniques for gathering this information consist of port scans, vulnerability scans, and/or wordlist scans utilizing tools that are introduced onto a system. (Citation: CISA AR21-126A FIVEHANDS May 2021) In cloud environments, adversaries might try to uncover services that are active on other cloud hosts. Moreover, if the cloud infrastructure is linked to an on-premises environment, adversaries could potentially recognize services that are running on non-cloud systems as well. In macOS environments, adversaries may leverage the built-in Bonjour application to detect services that are running on other macOS hosts within a network. The Bonjour mDNSResponder daemon automatically registers and promotes a host’s registered services across the network. For instance, adversaries can execute a mDNS query (such as dns-sd -B _ssh._tcp .) to locate other systems that are broadcasting the ssh service. ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Scheduled Task/Job

Adversaries can exploit the functionality of task scheduling to enable the initial or repeated execution of malicious code. All major operating systems provide utilities that allow for the scheduling of programs or scripts to run at predetermined dates and times. Additionally, a task may be set up on a remote system, assuming the necessary authentication is in place (e.g., RPC and file and printer sharing in Windows environments). Typically, scheduling a task on a remote machine requires membership in an administrative or otherwise privileged group on that system. (Citation: TechNet Task Scheduler Security)

Threat actors may leverage task scheduling to run programs at system startup or on a recurring schedule for persistence. Furthermore, these mechanisms can be manipulated to execute a process under the context of a specific account (such as one with elevated privileges). In a manner akin to [System Binary Proxy Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218), adversaries have also misused task scheduling to potentially conceal one-time executions within a trusted system process. (Citation: ProofPoint Serpent)

Attack description

An attacker can carry out a flooding attack employing the UDP protocol with the goal of preventing legitimate users from accessing a service by exhausting the available network bandwidth. Furthermore, firewalls typically open a port for each UDP connection directed toward a service that has an open UDP port, which means that firewalls effectively maintain the connection state; consequently, the high packet volume associated with a UDP flood can also overwhelm the resources assigned to the firewall. UDP attacks may also target services such as DNS or VoIP that rely on these protocols. Additionally, because of the session-less characteristic of the UDP protocol, it is relatively straightforward to spoof the source of a packet, complicating the task of identifying the attack's origin.

**Technique:** Exploit Public-Facing Application

Adversaries might try to take advantage of a vulnerability in a host or system that is accessible over the Internet in order to gain initial entry into a network. This vulnerability may stem from a software flaw, a transient error, or a misconfiguration.

The applications that are exploited frequently include websites or web servers, but they can also consist of databases (such as SQL), standard services (like SMB or SSH), management protocols for network devices (including SNMP and Smart Install), and any other systems that feature open sockets accessible via the Internet. (Citation: NVD CVE-2016-6662) (Citation: CIS Multiple SMB Vulnerabilities) (Citation: US-CERT TA18-106A Network Infrastructure Devices 2018) (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks) (Citation: NVD CVE-2014-7169) In the context of ESXi infrastructure, adversaries could exploit OpenSLP services that are exposed, or they might target unprotected VMware vCenter servers. When applications are hosted on cloud infrastructure or are containerized, exploiting them could lead to the compromise of the underlying instance or container. This can provide adversaries with a means to access cloud or container APIs (for instance, through the [Cloud Instance Metadata API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005)), exploit access to the container host using [Escape to Host](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611), or exploit weak identity and access management policies.

**Technique:** ARP Cache Poisoning

Threat actors can manipulate Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) caches to insert themselves into the communication path between multiple networked devices. This tactic may facilitate subsequent actions such as [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040) or [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002).

The ARP protocol serves to map IPv4 addresses to link layer addresses, like media access control (MAC) addresses. Devices within the same local network segment communicate using these link layer addresses. When a networked device lacks the link layer address for another device, it can issue a broadcast ARP request across the local network to convert the IP address into a MAC address. The device that holds the corresponding IP address responds directly with its MAC address. The device that initiated the ARP request will then utilize and retain this information in its ARP cache.

An attacker may wait passively for an ARP request to corrupt the ARP cache of the requesting device. By responding with their own MAC address, the adversary misleads the victim into thinking they are in communication with the correct networked device. To effectively poison the ARP cache, the adversary’s response must arrive faster than that of the legitimate owner of the IP address. Additionally, adversaries can issue a gratuitous ARP reply that falsely claims ownership of a specific IP address, broadcasting this to all devices within the local network segment.

Since the ARP protocol operates in a stateless manner and lacks authentication, devices can mistakenly add or modify the MAC address associated with an IP address in their ARP cache. 

Adversaries may exploit ARP cache poisoning as a method to capture network traffic. This activity can be employed to gather and/or relay sensitive data, including credentials, particularly those transmitted over insecure, unencrypted protocols.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Direct Network Flood

Adversaries may seek to create a denial of service (DoS) by inundating a target with a substantial volume of network traffic. This DoS attack can impair both the availability and functionality of the affected system(s) and network. [Direct Network Flood](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498/001) occurs when one or more systems direct a large number of network packets towards the network of the targeted service. Nearly any network protocol can be utilized for flooding purposes. Stateless protocols like UDP or ICMP are frequently employed, although stateful protocols such as TCP may also be utilized.

Network flooding attacks against services and networks are often carried out using botnets. Large-scale botnets can produce a considerable volume of traffic from systems distributed throughout the global Internet. Adversaries may possess the capability to develop and manage their own botnet infrastructure or may opt to lease access to an existing botnet to execute an attack. In extreme scenarios involving distributed DoS (DDoS), a vast number of systems contribute to the flood, with each needing only to transmit a minimal amount of traffic to generate sufficient volume to overwhelm the target network. In these situations, differentiating DDoS traffic from genuine clients becomes exceptionally challenging. Botnets have played a role in some of the most notable DDoS flooding incidents, such as the series of attacks in 2012 aimed at major US banks. (Citation: USNYAG IranianBotnet March 2016)

**Technique:** ARP Cache Poisoning

Adversaries can compromise Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) caches to insert themselves into the communication flow between two or more connected devices. This approach may facilitate subsequent actions such as [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040) or [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002).

The ARP protocol serves the purpose of mapping IPv4 addresses to link layer addresses, commonly referred to as media access control (MAC) addresses. (Citation: RFC826 ARP) Devices within a local network segment engage in communication by utilizing link layer addresses. In cases where a networked device lacks the link layer address corresponding to a specific device, it may issue a broadcast ARP request to the local network to convert the IP address into a MAC address. The device that holds the relevant IP address will respond directly with its MAC address. Subsequently, the networked device that initiated the ARP request will employ and retain this information in its ARP cache.

An adversary might passively monitor for an ARP request to taint the ARP cache of the device making the request. They can respond with their own MAC address, thereby misleading the victim into believing they are communicating with the correct networked device. To successfully poison the ARP cache, the adversary's response must arrive more promptly than that of the legitimate owner of the IP address. Additionally, adversaries may dispatch a gratuitous ARP reply that falsely claims ownership of a specific IP address to all devices within the local network segment.

The ARP protocol operates in a stateless manner and lacks authentication requirements. Consequently, devices may incorrectly add or modify the MAC address associated with an IP address in their ARP cache. (Citation: Sans ARP Spoofing Aug 2003)(Citation: Cylance Cleaver)

Adversaries can exploit ARP cache poisoning to intercept network traffic. This tactic may be utilized to gather and/or forward data such as credentials, particularly those transmitted over insecure, unencrypted protocols. (Citation: Sans ARP Spoofing Aug 2003)

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** ARP Cache Poisoning

Adversaries may manipulate Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) caches to insert themselves into the communication pathway between two or more networked devices. This tactic can facilitate subsequent actions such as [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040) or [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002).

The ARP protocol serves the purpose of mapping IPv4 addresses to link layer addresses, which include media access control (MAC) addresses. Within a local network segment, devices communicate with one another by utilizing link layer addresses. Should a networked device lack the link layer address for a specific networked device, it may issue a broadcast ARP request to the local network to translate the associated IP address into a MAC address. The device that owns the relevant IP address will respond directly with its MAC address. Subsequently, the networked device that initiated the ARP request will use and save this information in its ARP cache.

An adversary might wait passively for an ARP request to exploit and poison the ARP cache of the requesting device. By responding with their own MAC address, the adversary misleads the victim into believing they are communicating with the correct networked device. In order for the adversary to successfully poison the ARP cache, their response must arrive more quickly than that of the legitimate owner of the IP address. Additionally, adversaries might issue a gratuitous ARP reply that falsely claims ownership of a specific IP address to all devices within the local network segment.

Given that the ARP protocol is stateless and does not necessitate authentication, devices can mistakenly add or update the MAC address associated with an IP address in their ARP cache. 

Adversaries may exploit ARP cache poisoning to intercept network traffic. This approach can be used to gather and/or relay sensitive data, such as credentials, particularly those transmitted over unencrypted and insecure protocols.

Furthermore, firewalls typically open a port for every UDP connection directed at a service that has an open UDP port, effectively saving the connection state. UDP attacks are capable of targeting services such as DNS or VoIP that rely on these protocols. **Technique:** Brute Force

Adversaries might employ brute force methods to gain entry to accounts when they have no knowledge of the passwords or when they have obtained password hashes. (Citation: TrendMicro Pawn Storm Dec 2020) In cases where the password for one or more accounts is unknown, an adversary may methodically guess the password through a repetitive or iterative approach. (Citation: Dragos Crashoverride 2018) The process of brute forcing passwords can occur either through engagement with a service that verifies the validity of those credentials or offline using previously acquired credential data, such as password hashes.

Credential brute forcing can occur at various stages during a compromise. For instance, adversaries might try to brute force access to [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) within a targeted environment, utilizing information gathered from other post-compromise activities like [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003), [Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087), or [Password Policy Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1201). Additionally, adversaries may integrate brute forcing operations with actions such as [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133) as part of their Initial Access strategy.

Should an adversary successfully guess the correct password but still be unable to log into a compromised account due to location-specific conditional access policies, they may alter their infrastructure until it aligns with the victim’s location to circumvent those policies. (Citation: ReliaQuest Health Care Social Engineering Campaign 2024)

**Technique:** Adversary-in-the-Middle

Adversaries may attempt to position themselves between two or more networked devices using an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) technique to support follow-on behaviors such as [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040), [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002), or replay attacks ([Exploitation for Credential Access](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1212)). By abusing features of common networking protocols that can determine the flow of network traffic (e.g. ARP, DNS, LLMNR, etc.), adversaries may force a device to communicate through an adversary controlled system so they can collect information or perform additional actions.(Citation: Rapid7 MiTM Basics)

For example, adversaries may manipulate victim DNS settings to enable other malicious activities such as preventing/redirecting users from accessing legitimate sites and/or pushing additional malware.(Citation: ttint_rat)(Citation: dns_changer_trojans)(Citation: ad_blocker_with_miner) Adversaries may also manipulate DNS and leverage their position in order to intercept user credentials, including access tokens ([Steal Application Access Token](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528)) and session cookies ([Steal Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539)).(Citation: volexity_0day_sophos_FW)(Citation: Token tactics) [Downgrade Attack](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1689)s can also be used to establish an AiTM position, such as by negotiating a less secure, deprecated, or weaker version of communication protocol (SSL/TLS) or encryption algorithm.(Citation: mitm_tls_downgrade_att)(Citation: taxonomy_downgrade_att_tls)(Citation: tlseminar_downgrade_att)

Adversaries may also leverage the AiTM position to attempt to monitor and/or modify traffic, such as in [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002). **Technique:** Direct Network Flood

Adversaries may attempt to cause a denial of service (DoS) by directly sending a high-volume of network traffic to a target. This DoS attack may also reduce the availability and functionality of the targeted system(s) and network. [Direct Network Flood](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498/001)s are when one or more systems are used to send a high-volume of network packets towards the targeted service's network. Almost any network protocol may be used for flooding. Stateless protocols such as UDP or ICMP are commonly used but stateful protocols such as TCP can be used as well.

Botnets are commonly used to conduct network flooding attacks against networks and services. Large botnets can generate a significant amount of traffic from systems spread across the global Internet. Adversaries may have the resources to build out and control their own botnet infrastructure or may rent time on an existing botnet to conduct an attack. In some of the worst cases for distributed DoS (DDoS), so many systems are used to generate the flood that each one only needs to send out a small amount of traffic to produce enough volume to saturate the target network. In such circumstances, distinguishing DDoS traffic from legitimate clients becomes exceedingly difficult. Botnets have been used in some of the most high-profile DDoS flooding attacks, such as the 2012 series of incidents that targeted major US banks.(Citation: USNYAG IranianBotnet March 2016)
